To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the calcium currents of type I hair cells are activated by low depolarizing steps, are sensitive to nimodopine, are blocked by cadmium and are not inactivated at holding potentials between 60 and -100 mV.
the calcium current in type I vestibular hair cells is of the L type.
calcium current in type I semicircular canal hair cells has the characteristics of the L type.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the Ca( 2+) channels in type I hair cell.
the mechanisms involved in neurotransmitter release at type I hair cell afferent synapses.
the identification of the calcium current in type I vestibular hair cell and its possible role in neurotransmitter release.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neurotransmitter release is not mediated by low voltage-activated Ca(2+) channels in type I hair cell, and that other mechanism(s) must participate in this process.
the low voltage gain in hair cells is not a result of a specific Ca(2+) channel, but a consequence of the interaction of several factors.
neurotransmitter release in type I hair cell is not mediated by Ca(2+) channels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
type I hair cells have an L-type Ca(2+) channel that could participate in neurotransmitter release at the afferent synapses.
the low voltage gain in hair cells is due to low voltage activated calcium currents.
Ca(2+) channels are the main source of Ca(2+) influx in type I hair cell and that they are most likely of the low voltage activated type.

type I hair cells have L-type Ca(2+) currents, which are activated at the same potentials where the afferent synapses release neurotransmitter.
